Assess readiness to quit using the 5 As: Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, and Arrange.B
Individualized counseling, physician advice, tailored education messages, group interventions, motivational interviewing, supportive counseling, and telephone support are all effective.A

Options for first line drug therapy include bupropion, varenicline, nicotine gum, nicotine inhaler, nicotine nasal spray, and nicotine patch. American Thoracic Society guidelines recommend varenicline as first-line.A
Second line drug therapy options include clonidine or nortriptyline.B
Combination therapy with behavioral counseling and medication is more effective than either alone.B

background.definition: Smoking cessation, commonly known as "quitting" or "kicking the habit," is the effort to stop smoking tobacco products. Nicotine dependence can be one of the reasons patients seek counseling for smoking cessation.

list.listitem: Overall, 12.5% of Americans (18 years or older) smoke.

Prevalence varies by ethnic group: non-Hispanic American Indians/Alaska Natives (20.9%), non-Hispanic whites (15.5%), non-Hispanic Blacks (14.9%), Hispanics (8.8%), and non-Hispanic Asians (7.2%), non-Hispanic other races: 19.7% (includes non-Hispanic American Indian, Alaska native, and any other group or other single and multiple race persons).
Prevalence decreases with increases in education level and increased in mean household income.
Men are more likely to smoke (15.3%) compared to women (12.7%).
Total US expenditures estimated to be in excess of $600 billion in 2018.
Smoking was responsible for $240 billion in direct medical care for adults and $185 billion in lost productivity.
Smoking cessation programs are cost-effective.
Cigarette smoking is the leading cause of preventable death in the US, responsible for 1 out of every 5 deaths annually (480,000 deaths annually).
Cigarette smoking is a main risk factor in four leading causes of death: heart disease, cancer, stroke, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
Genetic predisposition
Environmental factors: peer influence, poor school performance, parental influence, media
Nicotine is a CNS stimulant.
Stimulating effects are exhibited mainly in the cortex.
Reward effects are mainly exhibited in the limbic system.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Peer influence, parental influence, poor school performance, risk-taking personality
Risk factors specific to adolescence in US: Caucasian race, no plan for higher degree, parental influence, peer influence, media, depression, ADD

list.listitem: Screen all adults at every visit for smoking cessation ("smoking as a vital sign").B

USPSTF recommends screening all non-pregnant and pregnant adults for tobacco abuse (Grade A), and recommends education and counseling to prevent initation of tobacco use in children and adolescents (Grade B).B
Assess readiness to quit using the 5 As: Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, and Arrange.B
Consider using the Fagerstrom Test to assess the degree of nicotine dependence ().C

As defined by the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed.; DSM–5; American Psychiatric Association, 2013) criteria, "tobacco use disorder" is a problematic pattern of tobacco use leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, as manifested by two or more of the following occuring within a 12 month period:
Tobacco is often taken in larger amounts or over a longer period that was intended
There is a persistent desire or unsuccessful efforts to cut down or control tobacco use
A great deal of time is spent in activities necessary to obtain or use tobacco
Craving, or a strong desire or urge to use tobacco
Recurrent tobacco use resulting in a failure to fulfill major role obligations at work, school, or home (e.g., interference with work)
Continued tobacco use despite having persistent or recurrent social or interpersonal problems caused or exacerbated by the effects of tobacco (e.g., arguments with others about tobacco use)
Important social, occupational, or recreational activities are given up or reduced because of tobacco use
Recurrent tobacco use in situations in which it is physically hazardous (e.g., smoking in bed)
Tobacco use is continued despite knowledge of having a persistent or recurrent physical or psychological problem that is likely to have been caused or exacerbated by tobacco

Tolerance, as defined by either of the following: (1) A need for markedly increased amounts of tobacco to achieve the desired effect (2) A markedly diminished effect with continued use of the same amount of tobacco

Withdrawal, as manifested by either of the following: (1) The characteristic withdrawal syndrome for tobacco (refer to Criteria A and B of the criteria set for tobacco withdrawal) (2) Tobacco (or a closely related substance, such as nicotine) is taken to relieve or avoid withdrawal symptoms
Assess readiness to quit using the 5 As: Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, and Arrange.

Ask patient if he or she is experiencing symptoms of withdrawal including: irritability/anger, mood changes, increased appetite, insomnia, weight gain, difficulty concentrating, anxiety, decreased heart rate.
Evaluate the patient for co-morbid conditions (i.e., COPD, asthma, diabetes, cancer, heart disease).
Ask about symptoms of shortness of breath, wheezing, difficulty breathing with activity, cough, or hemoptysis.
While nicotine levels can be used to assess tobacco use, they are not routinely recommended as part of a smoking cessation strategy.
The degree of nicotine dependence can be estimated using the Fagerstrom Test ().
Lung cancer risk can be evaluated by using a clinical decision rule.

Use the "5 As" approach: ask about smoking, advise patients to stop, assess motivation to stop and need for pharmacotherapy, assist with prescription or referral for behavioral medicine, and arrange follow-up.

If patient is willing to quit, offer assistance and/or medication. If patient is unsure, provide encouragement/motivation. If patient has already quit, prevent relapse. The degree of nicotine dependence can be estimated using the Fagerstrom Test ().
Quitting smoking improves rates of depression, measures of stress, and quality of life.
Individualized counseling, physician advice, tailored education messages,group interventions, motivational interviewing,supportive counseling and telephone support are all effective.A
Options for first line drug therapy include bupropion, varenicline, nicotine gum, nicotine inhaler, nicotine nasal spray, and nicotine patch.A
Varenicline appears to be more effective than nicotine replacement and bupropion SR and is recommended as first-line therapy by ATS guidelines.B
No benefit was found for varenicline alone or combined with NRT beyond 12 weeks.
Varenicline, bupropion, and NRT did not show increased neuropsychiatric adverse events compared to placebo in patients with stable psychiatric conditions.
Combination treatment with behavioral therapy plus medication is superior to either behavioral or medication treatment alone.B
The USPSTF recommends behavioral interventions and FDA-approved pharmacotherapy be offered to all non-pregnant adults who use tobacco.A

Options for first line therapy include nicotine replacement (NRT: gum, inhaler, nasal spray, patch), varenicline, and bupropion SR (). All forms of nicotine replacement therapy are equally effective compared to placebo (16.9% vs 10.5% six-month quit rates, RR 1.55 (95% CI 1.49-1.61). Combination NRT is more effective than single forms (16.9% vs 13.9%, RR 1.25 (95% CI 1.15-1.36) Limited evidence suggests that nicotine replacement may not be as effective in adolescents.

The American Thoracic Society guidelines (2020) recommend the use of varenicline (marketed in the United States as Chantix) monotherapy over all other agents, even among precontemplative patients and those with psychiatric conditions. Additionally, patients should be treated for longer than 12 weeks. The ATS also recommends varenicline plus nicotine replacement, but at the cost of increased side effects.
Gradual cessation and abrupt quitting produce comparable quit rates.
In motivated patients using nicotine replacement and undergoing behavioral counseling, abrupt quitting may be superior to gradual quitting (NNT = 13 at 1 month).

Varenicline appears to be more effective compared to bupropion and nicotine replacement.Continuous 52-week abstinence rates with varenicline versus bupropion in 3 trials (n = 1,618) had RR 1.52 (95% CI 1.22-1.88). When varenicline was compared to NRT, 24-week quit rates in 8 trials (n = 6,264) had RR 1.25 (95% CI 1.14-1.37).
Extending the prequit period in varenicline from 1 week to 4 weeks does not improve the quit rate.
Varenicline is superior to placebo in helping patients quit that prefer to "cut down" rather than quit "cold turkey" (NNT = 6).
A randomized trial found that extending the duration of prequit varenicline treatment from 1 week to 4 weeks before quitting did not improve successful abstinence rates of adult smokers.

A study found no additional benefit with varenicline plus NRT versus varenicline monotherapy, or with varenicline treatment for 24 weeks versus 12 weeks for increasing smoking cessation rates. These results were not affected by sex, race, treatment site, or level of tobacco dependence.
A Cochrane review concluded that among the antidepressants, bupropion and nortriptyline are effective to aid long-term smoking cessation. SSRIs do not aid long-term cessation.
Second-line therapy options include clonidine or nortriptyline. SSRIs such as fluoxetine and anxiolytics are not effective.
Even in patients who are not ready to quit, using nicotine patch helps some reduce smoking 6 months later.

Cytisine (not available in United States) is an inexpensive and effective option (NNT = 17 for abstinence at 12 months). A systematic review identified 12 RCTs of which 8 studies with 5922 participants compared it with placebo. It was more effective than placebo for cessation at the longest point of follow-up for each study (RR 2.25; 95% CI 1.42 - 3.56; NNT = 7).
A trial of cytisinicline to help adults stop vaping found efficacy after 12 weeks of treatment (32% vs 15%) but not a month later.
A trial randomizing 1452 adults to cytisine or varenicline found that quit rates for cytisine were not non-inferior to varenicline (11.7% vs 13.3%).
There is no evidence for the efficacy of lobeline, nicobrevin, silver acetate in aiding smoking cessation.
Smoking cessation therapies (NRT, bupropion, and varenicline) do not raise the risk of major cardiovascular events.

Combination treatment with behavioral therapy plus medication is superior to either behavioral or medication treatment alone. Bupropion plus nicotine replacement is no more effective than nicotine replacement alone.
Combination of varenicline for 12 weeks plus nicotine patch for 24 weeks in 446 adult smokers had higher quit rates than varenicline alone: Continuous abstinence rates at 24 weeks: 49% vs 32.6%
Combination NRT increases smoking cessation rates compared to single NRT treatment.
A RCT found that a 3 drug approach of patch, inhaler and bupropion was more effective than patch alone in medically ill smokers (NNT = 7) but was associated with higher rates of insomnia and anxiety.
Varenicline plus bupropion may have some short term benefits over varenicline alone but this benefit does not persist at 1 year. More patients experience anxiety and depression with the combination.
The combination of nicotine patch plus lozenge or gum was more effective than patch alone.

A randomized trial (n = 1792) compared a 4 week "preloading" with nicotine patch vs usual care and found a non-significant reduction in 6 month abstinence with preloading (17.5% vs 14.4%, p = 0.08). The nicotine group also was less likely to use varenicline post-randomization, which may have reduced long-term quitting.
Immediate reduction of nicotine in cigarettes was preferred over gradual reduction and led to greater reduction in detectable tobacco biomarkers compared to controls.

Subsequent therapy after initial cessation failureA randomized controlled trial with 490 adults who had initially failed varenicline or nicotine replacement demonstrated that increasing the dose of varenicline or combined nicotine replacment therapy (such as nicotine patch concentration) vs longer duration of either therapy may be effective for increasing quit rates after intial efforts failed..
A small study showed that patients prefer e-cigarettes to a nicotine inhaler.

A subsequent study with 884 smokers randomized to e-cigarette versus other nicotine based strategy, those randomized to e-cigarettes were more likely to have quit at one year (NNT = 12) but 40% were still using e-cigarettes at the end of the year.

An RCT compared nicotine e-cigarettes + counseling to non-nicotine e-cigarette + counseling to counseling alone. The nicotine e-cigarette group had improved abstinence at 12 weeks but no significant difference by week 24. The non-nicotine e-cigarette had a higher quit rate at 24 weeks (20.5% vs 9.9%, NNT = 10).

A systematic review with moderate certainty evidence compared e-cigarette with nicotine and nicotine replacement therapy for smoking cessation (3 RCTs, n = 1,498): Nicotine containing e-cigarettes were found superior (RR 1.69 95% CI 1.25-2.27) however more studies are needed to improve limitations and bias.
Vaping nicotine is more effective than NRT in inducing smoking cessation for people who smoke and have low socioeconomic status with NNT=5 for confirmed abstience at six months.
Use of e-cigarettes combined with standard smoking cessation therapies leads to significantly less use of tobacco at six months (29% vs 16%, NNT=6-8) but more use of nictotine (38% vs 23%, NNTH=8).

A study identified 458 community dwelling adults who had smoked for at least 10 years and randomized them to nicotine-containing e-cigarettes plus placebo, to varenicline plus nicotine-free e-cigarettes, or to placebo plus placebo. At 3 months quit rates were about 40% for both active therapy groups and 20% for placebo, but at 12 months abstinence was 38% for varenicline, 28% for e-cigarettes, and 20% for placebo.
Varenicline plus counseling is helpful to increase cesation rates for people who are attempting to quit vaping. (NNT=6 compared to placebo at both 12 and 24 weeks.)
Pre-operative smoking cessation improves surgical outcomes. A meta-analysis found that postoperative complications occurred in fewer patients who quit smoking (14% vs 28%, NNT = 7).
Quitting smoking within 8 weeks prior to surgery does not increase postoperative complications.
Perioperative smoking cessation interventions are effective at decreasing smoking at 1 year (NNT = 6).
Results from meta-analyses are mixed on the benefits of accupuncture. Evidence for hypnotherapy is insufficient or shows no benefit.
A small study of "self-massage" found may be effective but the study was poorly described.
There are no studies demonstrating effectiveness of the over the counter preparations "Nicobrevin" (quinine, menthyl valerate, camphor and eucalyptus oil) or silver acetate.
There is insufficient evidence to support exercise based interventions for smoking cessation but regular exercise has other health benefits.

Individualized counseling, physician advice, nurse-led behavioral interventions, and tailored education messages are effective.While group interventions are more effective than self-help, it is not known whether they are more effective than individual counseling. Non-medical partner support did not have any impact on increasing long-term abstinence from smoking.
The "teachable moment communication process" is challenging to implement in primary care practices but may provide some benefit.

Motivational interviewing is an empirically validated approach for smoking cessation and is more effective than brief advice alone. This model uses five phases to activate the patient: (1) Precontemplation (2) Contemplation (3) Preparation (4) Action, and (5) Relapse.
Meta-analysis of trials of supportive counseling found odds ratios of 1.6 (1.3-1.8) for individual support and 2 (1.6-2.6) for group support.

Evaluating lung function and then telling patients their "lung age" can increase quit rates (6.4% vs 13.6% at 6 months, NNT = 14). A Cochrane meta-analysis did not find evidence that providing smokers with feedback on their exposure to carbon monoxide, genetic susceptibility of smoking related disease, or effects of smoking on their health (i.e. spirometry, atherosclerotic plaque imaging) helped them quit smoking although some studies included were of low quality or high bias.
RCTs of telephone support also show effectiveness."Call back" counseling enhances telephone counseling usefullness.

RCT compared smartphone apps found ICan Quit smartphone app was better than QuitGuide app (28.2% quit rate at 12mo vs 21.1%). Translates to 1 additional smoker for every 14 who uses ICanQuit App rather than Quit Guide.
A simple pragmatic, employer based trial found higher (but still low) rates of smoking cesation with financial incentives added to free cessation aids.
Reward-based programs are much more accepted by employees than deposit-based incentive programs.
Customized text messages to mobile phones can help patients quit smoking (NNT = 17) and individually tailored web-based interventions can assist smoking cessation.
Smokers who quit smoking become less anxious.
Group based behavioral interventions are promising for helping adolescents quit smoking. More studies are needed for this special population.
Behavioral interventions were not found to be of benefit to help prevent relapse.
There is inadequate evidence to assess if exercise-based interventions in addition to counseling improve quit rates.
Weekly counseling is as effective as varenicline to help adolescents (age 17-21 years) quit smoking (8.9% quit rate in both groups).
Based on low level evidence, face-to-face behavioral support from community pharmacists may help people quit smoking.
Behavioral support from ex-smoking peers using instant messaging is effective compared to smoking cessation text messages.
E-cigarette text warnings are associated with reduced intentions to vape and increased intentions to quit vaping.
There is limited evidence on approaches to prevent weight gain when quitting smoking.

Combining smoking cessation with weight loss may improve the rate of smoking cessation in women. While in one study quit rates were greater in the group randomized to weight loss (28% vs 16%, NNT = 8) the amount of weight lost did not differ between groups.
School-based and workplace smoking cessation programs are of mixed effectiveness.

Mass media campaigns may be effective. When no other support is available, printed self-help material containing a structured program helped more peole to stop smoking. When oral advice from a healthcare professional or NRT was available, this benefit was lost.
Dual therapy with counseling and nicotine replacement therapy and/or varenicline may help hospitalized patients quit, but the effect may not be long-lasting.

Hospitaliation provides a unique opporutnity to address smoking cessation and according to a retrospective cohort stud is often underutilized as an opportunity to offer prescriptions for smoking cessation.

A post-hospital discharge smoking cessation intervention including interactive voice-response phone calls, optional behavioral counseling, and free access to smoking cessation medications improves smoking quit rates (NNT = 9).
Lung cancer screening with low-dose CT does not affect smoking quit rates.
While electronic medical record reminders can improve documentation of tobacco status and referral to counseling, it is not known if these reminders improve quit rates.
Smokers have typically stopped 7 to 20 times and most have tried several quit attempts before being successful.B
Better response rates are seen with length of visit more than 10 minutes; 4 or more visits; and more providers taking part in the intervention.A
Smokers live 5 to 10 years less than nonsmokers, on average.
Smokers have usually stopped multiple times and most have tried several quit attempts before being successful. Estimates range from 7 to 20 times trying before successfully quitting.
Meta-analyses indicate that frequent follow-up through phone support is useful.
An RCT and meta-analyses indicate that smokers are more likely to quit with combination therapy.
For patients with lung cancer (early stage), quitting smoking is associated with a longer lifespan.
Follow-up with patients after starting smoking cessation treatment, especially after starting new medication.
Re-assess patient after their quit date.
Better response rates are seen with length of visit more than 10 minutes; four or more visits; and more providers taking part in the intervention.
Recommend combined therapy (i.e., behavioral and medication) and set a quit date with patients.
Address coping strategies for smoking triggers.
Advise that patient may experience withdrawal symptoms, but that cravings will be short-lived and will decrease in severity and frequency over time.
Advise about health benefits of quitting.
Meta-analyses have shown that low birth weight and preterm deliveries are associated with smoking pregnant mothers.
Nicotine metabolism increases by 30% during pregnancy, which can affect treatment options.
Nicotine replacement therapy is effective to reduce smoking rates in pregnancy. Data so far does not indicate harms.
An RCT using nicotine gum showed that its use decreased the risk of preterm and low birthweight infants.
A meta-analysis of counseling interventions for pregnant smokers showed minimal benefit.
USPSTF recommends behavioral counseling for smoking cessation in pregnant patients (Grade A), with insufficient evidence for safety and efficacy for pharmacological therapy.
Nicotine replacement products are not approved for persons younger than 18 years old.
Children who use e-cigarettes are strongly likely to use traditional cigarettes later in life.
USPSTF recommends brief counseling to prevent smoking initiation (Grade B).

feature.caption: Fagerstrom Test for Nicotine Dependence.
feature.feature_body:
How soon after you wake up do you smoke your first cigarette?
After 60 min (0)
31-60 min (1)
6-30 min (2)
Within 5 min (3)
Do you find it difficult to refrain from smoking in places where it is forbidden?
No (0)
Yes (1)
Which cigarette would you hate most to give up?
The first in the morning (1)
Any other (0)
How many cigarettes per day do you smoke?
10 or less (0)
11-20 (1)
21-30 (2)
31 or more (3)
Do you smoke more frequently during the first hours after awakening than during the rest of the day?
No (0)
Yes (1)
Do you smoke even if you are so ill that you are in bed most of the day?
No (0)
Yes (1)
• Add up the score and interpret as follows: 0-2 very low dependence; 3-4 low dependence; 5 medium dependence; 6-7 high dependence; 8-10 very high dependence
From Heatherton TF, Kozlowski LT, Frecker RC, Fagerstrom KO. The Fagerstrom Test for nicotine dependence: a revision of the Fagerstrom Tolerance Questionnaire. Br J Addict 1991;86:1119–1127.

tr.td: Start 150 mg once daily for 3 d, and then increase to twice daily for 8 wk
Patient should be instructed to set their quit date1 wk after starting medication. Should take second dose in early evening to avoid decreased sleep
Patient should start the night before quitting. Patch placement site should be rotated every day to reduce skin reactions
Patches: start with 21-mg patch and taper over 4-6 wk
Apply patch to hairless skin, rotate sites. If skin reaction occurs, apply topical hydrocortisone
Lozenges or gum: start with 4-mg strength and taper

Chew gum until taste is apparent, then park in cheek. Chew intermittently for 30 minutes or until taste fades. Do not swallow saliva o help with dyspepsia. Do not eat or drink anything besides water for 15 minutes before or after gum/ lozenge. Common ADRs: hiccups, dyspepsia, heartburn
Patches; start with 14-mg patch and taper over 2-4 wk
Lozenges or gum: start with 2-mg strength and taper
Start at 0.5mg once daily for 3 d, and then taper up to 1 mg twice daily for 12-24 wk
Patient can smoke for the first week of treatment. Nausea is common and can be minimized by taking with food. Reduced dose can aid with nausea
Start with 25 mg and taper to 75 mg daily for 8-12 wk. Taper before discontinuing
Side effects usually tolerable with time
